events.title: Neolithic Settlement
events.description: Archaeological evidence shows human settlement in present-day Mauritania during the Neolithic period. The Sahara region was then more humid, supporting agriculture and pastoralism. Rock paintings and archaeological sites prove the existence of early inhabitants who engaged in hunting, gathering, and early agricultural activities. These early settlers laid the foundation for later civilizational development.

events.title: Beginning of Sahara Desertification
events.description: Climate change led to the beginning of desertification in the Sahara region, forcing populations to migrate south to more habitable areas. This process continued for thousands of years, completely transforming the region's ecological environment and population distribution. The desertification process promoted the development of nomadic lifestyles and influenced later social organizational forms.

events.title: Berber Settlement
events.description: Berber peoples began settling in the Mauritanian region, establishing early tribal organizations. They developed lifestyles adapted to desert environments, including nomadic pastoralism and trans-Saharan trade. The arrival of Berbers marked important changes in the region's culture and social structure, with their language and culture having profound influence on later development.

events.title: Early Trans-Saharan Trade
events.description: The Mauritanian region began participating in early trans-Saharan trade networks. Merchants transported salt, gold, ivory, and slaves, connecting North Africa and sub-Saharan Africa. The development of these trade routes promoted economic prosperity and cultural exchange, creating conditions for the later rise of large trading empires.

events.title: Indirect Roman Influence
events.description: Although the Roman Empire never directly controlled Mauritania, Roman culture and goods indirectly influenced the region through Roman provinces in North Africa. Roman coins and artifacts have been found in archaeological sites, proving the connection between trans-Saharan trade and the Mediterranean world. Trade during this period promoted regional economic development and cultural exchange.

events.title: Tribal Confederation Period
events.description: After the Almohad Dynasty's decline, Mauritania entered a period of tribal confederation rule. Various Berber and Arab tribes established loose alliances, controlling different regions and trade routes. This period was characterized by political decentralization, but trade and cultural exchange remained active. Competition and cooperation between tribes shaped the region's unique social structure.

events.title: Timbuktu Academic Connections
events.description: Mauritanian scholars and merchants maintained close connections with the famous academic center of Timbuktu. Cities like Walata and Chinguetti became important centers of Islamic learning, attracting students from across West Africa. Manuscripts and scholarly traditions from this period are still preserved in Mauritanian libraries, proving the region's rich intellectual heritage.

events.title: Songhai Empire Period
events.description: The Songhai Empire expanded under Askia Muhammad, influencing southern Mauritanian regions. The empire controlled important trade cities and routes, promoting economic prosperity. Songhai Empire's administrative systems and Islamic legal practices influenced the region's political and social organization. The empire's decline created conditions for further Arab tribal migration.

events.title: European Trade Competition
events.description: Portugal, Spain, Netherlands, France, and Britain successively established trading posts on the Mauritanian coast, competing for control of trans-Atlantic trade. Main trade goods included gold, gum arabic, slaves, and salt. European arrival changed local economic structures, but inland tribal societies remained largely independent. Coastal trade development promoted wealth and power growth of certain tribes.

events.title: Chinguetti Academic Golden Age
events.description: Chinguetti became one of West Africa's major centers of Islamic learning, called 'the Sorbonne of the desert.' The city had numerous mosques, libraries, and schools, training many famous Islamic scholars. Chinguetti's manuscript collections contain works of jurisprudence, theology, astronomy, and literature, becoming precious cultural heritage.

events.title: Ghana Empire Rule
events.description: The Ghana Empire (Wagadou Empire) controlled vast territories including southeastern Mauritania. The empire's capital Koumbi Saleh was located in present-day Mauritania and served as an important trading and political center. Ghana Empire accumulated enormous wealth by controlling gold and salt trade, becoming one of West Africa's most powerful political entities. The empire's rule promoted urban development, craft prosperity, and cultural exchange.

events.title: Rock Art Flourishing
events.description: The Adrar Plateau and other regions of Mauritania preserve rich rock art depicting hunting scenes, animals, human activities, and religious rituals. These rock paintings reflect the lifestyle, beliefs, and artistic expression of contemporary inhabitants. Rock art is important material for studying the region's prehistoric and early history, showing environmental changes from humid climate to desertification.

events.title: Formation of Berber Kingdoms
events.description: Berber tribes established multiple small kingdoms and chiefdoms in the Mauritanian region. These political entities controlled important trade routes and oases, developing complex social organizations and military systems. The formation of Berber kingdoms marked the region's transition from tribal society to more complex political structures, laying foundations for later large empire rise.

events.title: Introduction of Islam
events.description: Through trans-Saharan trade and Arab merchant activities, Islam began entering Mauritania. Initially spreading mainly among merchants and ruling classes, it gradually influenced local religious, legal, and social systems. The introduction of Islam brought Arabic script, Islamic jurisprudence, and new architectural styles, profoundly changing local culture.

events.title: Rise of Almoravid Dynasty
events.description: The Berber-established Almoravid Dynasty (Murabitun) controlled most of Mauritania and Morocco. The dynasty originated from a religious reform movement in Mauritania, led by Abdullah ibn Yasin. The Almoravids established a strict Islamic state, promoted Maliki jurisprudence, and controlled important trade routes. Their rule promoted the development of Islamic education and culture.

events.title: Almohad Dynasty Rule
events.description: The Almohad Dynasty (Muwahhidun) replaced the Almoravids, controlling the Maghreb region including Mauritania. The dynasty promoted stricter Islamic doctrine, fostering religious unity and cultural development. Under their rule, the Islamization process in Mauritania accelerated, with Arabic language and Islamic culture spreading further.

events.title: Rise of Walata Commercial Center
events.description: Walata became an important commercial and academic center, serving as a key node in trans-Saharan trade. The city attracted merchants and scholars from North Africa, Middle East, and sub-Saharan Africa. Walata's mosques and schools became important centers of Islamic learning, training many famous scholars and jurists. The city's prosperity lasted for several centuries.

events.title: Mali Empire Influence
events.description: The powerful Mali Empire under Mansa Musa reached its zenith, with influence extending to eastern and southern Mauritanian regions. The Mali Empire promoted prosperity of trans-Saharan trade, particularly gold and salt trade. The empire's Islamization policies and scholarly traditions influenced Mauritania's cultural development, promoting Islamic education and Arabic language spread.

events.title: First Portuguese Arrival
events.description: Portuguese explorer Nuno Tristão first reached the Mauritanian coast, marking the first European contact with the region. The Portuguese were primarily interested in gold, ivory, and slave trade. They established trading posts on the coast, but inland areas remained under local tribal control. This contact opened the prelude to European colonialism in West Africa.

events.title: Great Arab Tribal Migration
events.description: Large numbers of Arab tribes migrated from the east to Mauritania, particularly the arrival of Maqil Arabs. These nomadic tribes brought new culture, language, and social organizational forms. The Arabization process accelerated, with Arabic gradually becoming the dominant language. Tribal social structures were strengthened, forming complex social hierarchies.

events.title: French Establish Saint-Louis Trading Post
events.description: France established the Saint-Louis trading post at the mouth of the Senegal River, beginning to influence southern Mauritania. French merchants established trade relations with local tribes, mainly trading gum arabic, leather, and slaves. Saint-Louis became an important base for French expansion in West Africa, laying the foundation for later colonial rule.

events.title: Moroccan Sultanate Influence
events.description: Morocco's Alaouite dynasty attempted to expand influence over northern Mauritanian regions. Although unable to establish direct rule, the Moroccan Sultan had important religious and cultural influence on the region. Some tribes recognized the Moroccan Sultan's religious authority, and this connection continued to influence later political development.

events.title: Char Bouba War
events.description: A prolonged conflict erupted between Berber tribes (Sanhaja) and Arab tribes (Hassan), known as the 'Char Bouba War.' This war established Arab tribal dominance in military and political matters, while Berber tribes maintained influence in religious and academic fields. The war's outcome shaped Mauritania's unique social hierarchy system, forming a division between warrior class (Hassan) and religious scholar class (Zawaya).

events.title: Gum Arabic Trade Prosperity
events.description: Mauritania became the world's major gum arabic producer, this resin having important uses in European industry. Gum arabic trade brought enormous wealth to local tribes, changing socio-economic structures. French merchants controlled most export trade, strengthening French influence in the region. Trade prosperity promoted coastal city development.

events.title: Wreck of the Medusa
events.description: The French naval frigate Medusa ran aground and sank near the Mauritanian coast, with survivors' tragedy on a raft shocking Europe. This event inspired French painter Géricault to create the famous painting 'The Raft of the Medusa.' The event also prompted France to pay more attention to navigation safety along this coastline, indirectly promoting French colonial activities in the region.

events.title: Early Moorish-French Contact
events.description: French colonizers began establishing closer contact with Mauritanian Moorish tribes from their Senegal base. France gradually infiltrated the region through protection treaties, trade agreements, and military alliances. Diplomatic and military activities during this period laid foundations for later complete conquest, while also causing divisions among tribes about whether to cooperate with France.

events.title: French Colonial Expansion
events.description: France began systematically expanding its influence in Mauritania, gradually controlling coastal and inland areas through military conquest and treaty signing. French Governor Louis Faidherbe promoted this expansion process. Local tribes conducted fierce resistance, but French modern weapons and tactics ultimately gained advantage. This period marked the transition from traditional tribal society to colonial rule.

events.title: Complete French Conquest
events.description: French forces under Colonel Xavier Coppolani completed the conquest of Mauritania. Coppolani established the first French military post in 1902, and Mauritania officially became a French colony in 1912. The conquest process encountered fierce tribal resistance, particularly from Maqil Arab tribes. The establishment of French rule completely changed the region's political and social structures.

events.title: Establishment of French Mauritania
events.description: France formally established the French Mauritania colony, becoming part of French West Africa federation. The colonial government implemented direct rule, introducing French administrative systems, education, and legal systems. Traditional tribal structures were weakened but not completely eliminated. Colonial rule brought modern infrastructure construction but also intensified social inequality.

events.title: Colonial Economic Development
events.description: The French colonial government developed an economy based on raw material exports, with main products including gum arabic, leather, salt, and fish. The colonial government built roads, ports, and telegraph lines, improving transportation and communication. However, economic development primarily served French interests, with limited benefits for local people. Implementation of forced labor systems caused widespread discontent.

events.title: Pacification of Adrar and Tagant
events.description: French colonial forces completed pacification of the last resisting tribes in the Adrar Plateau and Tagant regions. These remote nomadic tribes had resisted French rule but were eventually conquered by modernized military. France established administrative posts and military garrisons in these regions, marking consolidation of colonial rule throughout Mauritania.

events.title: Site Selection for Nouakchott
events.description: The French colonial government began considering establishing a new administrative center on the Atlantic coast. At the time, Mauritania's main cities were inland, and France wanted to establish a coastal city more convenient for control and external communication. Although construction would not officially begin until after independence, site selection work had already started during this period, laying foundations for the future capital.

events.title: Vichy France Rule
events.description: During World War II, French Mauritania was under Vichy France rule. Economic difficulties intensified during this period, with the colonial government increasing exploitation of local resources. The war also exposed limitations of French power, planting seeds for later independence movements. Some Mauritanians joined Free French forces, playing roles in the war.

events.title: Post-WWII Political Awakening
events.description: After World War II, new political consciousness emerged in Mauritania. African soldiers who had participated in the war brought back new ideas, and France's weakening during the war also inspired independence demands. The first modern political organizations began forming, and French-educated elites began demanding more political rights. This period marked the beginning of nationalist movements.

events.title: First African Representative Elections
events.description: Under the new French constitutional framework, Mauritania held its first elections for representatives to the French National Assembly. Although voting rights were strictly limited, this marked the beginning of local people's participation in political decision-making processes. These early elections cultivated the first generation of political leaders for later democratic development.

events.title: French Union Status
events.description: After the war, Mauritania gained overseas territory status within the French Union. The new constitution granted limited autonomy and established local assemblies. Though limited, this reform provided space for political participation and nationalist movement development. Increased educational opportunities cultivated a new generation of political leaders.

events.title: Iron Ore Exploration
events.description: French geologists discovered rich iron ore resources in the Zouérat region of northern Mauritania. This discovery would have profound impact on the country's future economic development. France began planning mineral development and related infrastructure construction, including railways and ports. The iron ore discovery greatly increased Mauritania's economic importance.

events.title: Slavery Abolition Decree
events.description: The French colonial government issued a decree officially abolishing slavery in Mauritania. However, this decree encountered major obstacles in implementation, as slavery was deeply rooted in local social structures. Many traditional elites resisted this reform, and slavery actually continued in various forms in many regions. This issue would continue to trouble post-independence Mauritania.

events.title: Internal Autonomy
events.description: Under France's Loi-Cadre, Mauritania gained internal autonomy status, establishing a semi-autonomous government. Moktar Ould Daddah became head of government, later becoming the first president after independence. This reform accelerated the decolonization process, preparing for complete independence.

events.title: Islamic Republic Declaration
events.description: In de Gaulle's constitutional referendum, Mauritania chose to become an autonomous republic within the French Community, declaring itself an Islamic Republic. This decision reflected the country's religious character and cultural identity. Mauritania became the first modern state to be named an Islamic Republic.

events.title: Mauritanian Independence
events.description: Mauritania formally gained independence from France, with Moktar Ould Daddah becoming the first president. Independence celebrations were held in the capital Nouakchott, marking the end of French colonial rule in the region. The new nation faced enormous challenges of building modern state institutions, developing the economy, and maintaining national unity.

events.title: Iron Ore Development
events.description: Mauritania began large-scale development of Zouérat iron ore, which became the backbone of the national economy. French and other European companies invested in building mines, railways, and port facilities. Iron ore exports brought important revenue to the country but also deepened dependence on foreign investment and technology. Mining development changed the country's economic structure.

events.title: Moroccan Territorial Dispute
events.description: Morocco claimed sovereignty over Mauritania, refusing to recognize its independence, claiming Mauritania was part of 'Greater Morocco.' This dispute led to long-term diplomatic tensions, affecting Mauritania's international status. The Arab League initially supported Morocco's position until recognizing Mauritania in 1969.

events.title: Joining the United Nations
events.description: Mauritania joined the United Nations, gaining international recognition. However, due to Moroccan opposition, the joining process was not smooth. The Soviet Union initially vetoed Mauritania's membership application until Morocco agreed to Mongolia's UN membership, after which Mauritania successfully joined. This marked the establishment of the country's international status.

events.title: Monetary Reform
events.description: Mauritania withdrew from the franc zone and issued its own currency, the ouguiya. This decision reflected the country's desire for economic independence but also brought monetary instability and inflation problems. Monetary reform was an important component of Daddah government's economic nationalism policies.

events.title: Sahel Drought Disaster
events.description: Severe drought struck the Sahel region, including Mauritania. The drought caused massive famine, livestock deaths, and population migration. Traditional nomadic lifestyles were severely impacted, with many herders forced to migrate to cities. This disaster exposed the country's economic vulnerability and sensitivity to climate change.

events.title: Western Sahara Conflict Begins
events.description: After Spain withdrew from Western Sahara, Mauritania signed the Madrid Accords with Morocco, partitioning Western Sahara territory. Mauritania gained the southern region but faced armed resistance from the Polisario Front. This decision embroiled Mauritania in prolonged military conflict, consuming enormous national resources.

events.title: Military Coup Overthrows Daddah
events.description: Military officers staged a coup, overthrowing President Moktar Ould Daddah. The main reasons for the coup were failures in the Western Sahara war and economic difficulties. Colonel Mustapha Ould Salek became the new head of state. The coup marked Mauritania's entry into a period of military rule.

events.title: Withdrawal from Western Sahara
events.description: Under military pressure and economic difficulties, Mauritania signed a peace agreement with the Polisario Front, abandoning territorial claims to Western Sahara and recognizing the Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic. This decision ended the costly war but also caused Moroccan displeasure. Mauritanian forces withdrew from Western Sahara.

events.title: Haidalla Military Coup
events.description: Colonel Mohamed Khouna Ould Haidalla staged a coup, overthrowing the Salek government. Haidalla promised economic reforms and political opening but actually established more authoritarian rule. His government faced challenges including economic crisis, ethnic tensions, and political instability.

events.title: Intensifying Ethnic Tensions
events.description: Ethnic tensions intensified between Arab-Berber people (Bidhan) and Black Africans (Haratin and Black Mauritanians) in Mauritania. The government's Arabization policies caused discontent in Black communities. Language policy, land rights, and political representation became contentious issues. These tensions laid the groundwork for later ethnic conflicts.

events.title: Taya Military Coup
events.description: Colonel Maaouya Ould Sid'Ahmed Taya staged a coup while Haidalla was abroad, seizing power. Taya established the Military Committee for National Salvation, promising economic reforms and political stability. His rule would last over 20 years, making him the longest-serving leader in Mauritanian history.

events.title: Arabic Becomes Sole Official Language
events.description: The Taya government declared Arabic as Mauritania's sole official language, removing French's official status. This decision was an important component of Arabization policies but caused strong opposition from Black communities. Language policy became an important source of ethnic tensions, intensifying social divisions.

events.title: Mauritania-Senegal Border Conflict
events.description: Mauritania and Senegal erupted in serious conflict due to border disputes and ethnic tensions. The conflict led to massive population displacement, with hundreds of thousands forced to leave their homes. Mauritania's Black population suffered persecution, with many fleeing to Senegal. This event was called Mauritania's 'ethnic cleansing,' severely damaging the country's international image.

events.title: Economic Structural Adjustment
events.description: With World Bank and International Monetary Fund support, Mauritania implemented economic structural adjustment programs. Reforms included privatization, trade liberalization, and public spending cuts. These measures improved macroeconomic indicators but also intensified social inequality and unemployment problems.

events.title: New Constitution and Multi-party System
events.description: Under domestic and international pressure, the Taya government promulgated a new constitution, establishing a multi-party democratic system. The constitution guaranteed basic rights and freedoms, but Taya actually maintained control of political power. Opposition parties were allowed to exist but faced various restrictions. This reform was an important milestone in Mauritania's political development.

events.title: First Multi-party Elections
events.description: Mauritania held its first multi-party presidential and parliamentary elections since independence. Taya won the presidential election, but the electoral process was questioned by the opposition. Despite controversies, the elections marked the country's transition toward democratic institutions. International observers expressed concerns about the freedom and fairness of elections.

events.title: Taya Re-elected President
events.description: Taya won re-election in the presidential election, but the election was again questioned by the opposition and criticized by the international community. The opposition alleged electoral fraud and government manipulation. Despite this, Taya continued to pursue economic reform and political opening policies.

events.title: International Attention on Slavery Issue
events.description: International human rights organizations began focusing on Mauritania's slavery problem. Although the government officially abolished slavery in 1981, this practice still existed in reality, particularly in rural areas. International pressure prompted the government to take more measures to combat modern slavery.

events.title: Taya's Third Re-election
events.description: Taya won a third victory in the presidential election, but the electoral process was again questioned. Opposition and international observers pointed out unfair phenomena in the election. Taya's long-term rule caused increasing discontent, laying groundwork for later political changes.

events.title: Military Coup Overthrows Taya
events.description: Military officers staged a coup, overthrowing President Taya. The coup was led by Colonel Ely Ould Mohamed Vall, establishing the Military Council for Justice and Democracy. The coup received widespread popular support as people were tired of Taya's long-term rule. The military government promised democratic transition.

events.title: Constitutional Referendum
events.description: The military government organized a constitutional referendum, with the new constitution limiting presidential terms to two, strengthening parliamentary powers, and guaranteeing basic rights. The referendum passed with an overwhelming majority, laying legal foundation for democratic transition. The new constitution was considered important progress in Mauritania's democratic development.

events.title: Sidi Ould Cheikh Abdallahi Elected President
events.description: In presidential elections held under international supervision, Sidi Ould Cheikh Abdallahi won, becoming Mauritania's first democratically elected president. The election was considered free and fair by the international community, marking successful democratic transition. Abdallahi promised to advance democratic reforms and economic development.

events.title: Aziz Military Coup
events.description: General Mohamed Ould Abdel Aziz staged a coup, overthrowing President Abdallahi. Reasons for the coup included disagreements between government and military as well as economic policy disputes. Aziz established the High State Council, promising to hold new elections. This coup interrupted Mauritania's democratic process.

events.title: Aziz Elected President
events.description: In a controversial presidential election, Aziz won and became president. The opposition boycotted the election, and the international community questioned the election's legitimacy. Despite this, the Aziz government gradually gained international recognition. He promised to advance economic development and fight corruption.

events.title: War on Terror
events.description: Mauritania faced threats from Islamic extremist groups in the Sahel region, particularly Al-Qaeda in the Islamic Maghreb. The government strengthened security measures and cooperated with the international community to combat terrorism. The war on terror became an important component of national security policy, affecting political and social development.

events.title: Aziz Re-elected President
events.description: Aziz won re-election in the presidential election, but the electoral process was again questioned by the opposition. The opposition alleged electoral fraud, but international observers considered the election basically met international standards. Aziz's re-election ensured political stability but also raised concerns about democratic quality.

events.title: Mohamed Ould Ghazouani Elected President
events.description: In Mauritania's first peaceful power transition in history, Mohamed Ould Ghazouani was elected president. Ghazouani was Aziz's former defense minister, representing the ruling party. The election was considered relatively free and fair, marking the maturity of the country's democratic institutions.

events.title: COVID-19 Pandemic Impact
events.description: The COVID-19 pandemic severely impacted Mauritania, with the government implementing lockdown measures and travel restrictions. The pandemic intensified economic difficulties, particularly for poor populations dependent on informal economy. The government launched economic relief programs, but resources were limited. The pandemic exposed vulnerabilities in the national health system.

events.title: Slavery Criminalization Law
events.description: Mauritania passed new legislation defining slavery as a crime against humanity, increasing penalties for slavery. This legislation was passed under international pressure, aimed at more effectively combating modern slavery. However, enforcement still faces challenges, particularly in remote rural areas.

events.title: Natural Gas Discovery
events.description: Large natural gas reserves were discovered in Mauritanian waters, bringing new opportunities for national economic development. The government signed development agreements with international energy companies, with gas exports expected to begin in coming years. This discovery could change the country's economic structure, reducing dependence on traditional industries.

events.title: Local Elections
events.description: Mauritania held local elections, with the ruling party winning in most regions. The electoral process was relatively calm, but voter turnout was low. Local elections were seen as a test of support for Ghazouani's government, with results showing the government still enjoyed considerable popular support.

events.title: Ongoing Development Challenges
events.description: Mauritania still faces numerous development challenges, including poverty, inequality, climate change, and modern slavery. Despite hopes brought by gas discoveries, the country still needs structural reforms to achieve sustainable development. The government is committed to improving education, healthcare, and infrastructure, but progress is slow. Ethnic reconciliation, democratic consolidation, and economic diversification remain major challenges. The international community continues to support Mauritania's development efforts, but the country's future largely depends on its ability to effectively utilize natural resources and build an inclusive society.
